# Clean Architecture — Accelerated Engineering Leadership Course

Intermediate to Advanced · 2–3 hours · Technical Lead / Principal Engineer / Software Architect / Engineering Manager

## Course objective

Clean Architecture is not primarily about organizing code into projects, adding interfaces, or implementing repositories. It is about **controlling dependencies, protecting business logic, and designing software that can evolve without unnecessary coupling to infrastructure or delivery mechanisms.**

At the senior engineering level, the challenge is not understanding how to implement Clean Architecture. It is knowing **when its separation of concerns creates business value, when it introduces unnecessary complexity, and how to apply it consistently across an engineering organization.**

This course uses enterprise examples involving C\#, .NET, Azure, SQL Server, messaging, and distributed services.

## Learning roadmap

**Estimated study time** 160 minutes

---

# Module 1 — Clean Architecture fundamentals

30 minutes

## 1.1 What is Clean Architecture?

Clean Architecture is a software design approach popularized by Robert C. Martin that organizes systems around business rules and use cases rather than databases, frameworks, or external interfaces.

Its central principle is\:

**Source-code dependencies should point toward the business rules, not outward toward infrastructure.**

Consider a financial platform responsible for processing customer transactions.

The system might use\:

- ASP.NET Core to expose APIs.
- SQL Server to store transactions.
- Kafka to publish transaction events.
- Redis for caching.
- Azure for hosting and secrets management.

These are implementation technologies. They are not the fundamental business purpose of the system.

The actual business capabilities include validating transactions, applying business rules, maintaining balances, and enforcing authorization policies.

Clean Architecture attempts to prevent those capabilities from becoming unnecessarily dependent on the surrounding technologies.

### The conceptual architecture

```svg
<svg viewBox="0 0 340 280" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="8" y="8" width="324" height="264" rx="20" fill="#9BB9D4" fill-opacity=".18" stroke="#7697B7" /><rect x="36" y="35" width="268" height="209" rx="20" fill="#75A4C9" fill-opacity=".22" stroke="#6492B7" /><rect x="67" y="65" width="206" height="151" rx="20" fill="#4F87BA" fill-opacity=".24" stroke="#487AA7" /><rect x="103" y="99" width="134" height="84" rx="18" fill="#2367A0" stroke="#205C8F" /><g font-size="12" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle"><text x="170" y="25" fill="currentColor">Frameworks & Infrastructure</text><text x="170" y="52" fill="currentColor">Interface Adapters</text><text x="170" y="84" fill="currentColor">Application Use Cases</text><text x="170" y="137" fill="#FFFFFF">Domain</text><text x="170" y="153" fill="#FFFFFF">Business Rules</text></g><g stroke="#256DA8" stroke-width="2" fill="none" stroke-linecap="round"><path d="M170 224 V189" /><path d="M165 195 L170 188 L175 195" /><path d="M54 144 H94" /><path d="M88 139 L95 144 L88 149" /><path d="M286 144 H246" /><path d="M252 139 L245 144 L252 149" /></g><text x="170" y="259" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10">Source-code dependencies point inward</text></svg>
```

Conceptual dependency model, not a mandatory folder structure.

The inner layers represent more stable business policies. Outer layers contain implementation details that are more likely to change.

The important distinction is that **runtime execution may flow outward, even while source-code dependencies point inward.**

For example, a use case can call an interface whose implementation writes to SQL Server. The application layer owns the interface, while the infrastructure layer provides its implementation.

## 1.2 Why Clean Architecture exists

Enterprise applications frequently begin with a straightforward implementation\:

```text
API Controller
    ↓
Business Service
    ↓
Entity Framework DbContext
    ↓
SQL Server
```

This is not inherently bad.

Problems emerge when business logic becomes entangled with the database, framework, transport, and operational concerns.

Imagine a transaction-processing service where a controller\:

1. Validates business rules.
2. Queries SQL Server directly.
3. Updates account balances.
4. Publishes Kafka messages.
5. Sends notification emails.
6. Handles retry logic.

Initially, this may be efficient to implement.

Over time, however, the team discovers that\:

- Business rules are duplicated across endpoints.
- Database schema changes affect unrelated code.
- Testing requires extensive infrastructure setup.
- Messaging failures leave data inconsistent.
- New developers struggle to locate business behavior.
- Reusing the capability in background workers becomes difficult.

Clean Architecture addresses these problems by establishing boundaries between responsibilities.

It does not automatically eliminate complexity. It attempts to make complexity more manageable and changes more localized.

## 1.3 The five essential principles

| Principle | Meaning |
|--------|--------|
| Separation of concerns | Different responsibilities have explicit boundaries |
| Dependency inversion | Business policies depend on abstractions rather than concrete infrastructure |
| Framework independence | Business logic is not inherently tied to ASP.NET Core, EF Core, or Azure |
| Testability | Core behavior can be verified without starting the entire system |
| Change isolation | Changes to one implementation detail should have limited impact on unrelated business behavior |

### Dependency inversion is the most important

Consider two designs.

**Infrastructure-dependent design**

```text
OrderService
    ↓
SqlOrderRepository
    ↓
SQL Server
```

The business service depends directly on a SQL-specific implementation.

**Dependency-inverted design**

```text
OrderService
    ↓
IOrderRepository
    ↑
SqlOrderRepository
```

The application defines the contract it requires.

Infrastructure implements that contract.

This means the application controls its dependencies rather than allowing infrastructure to dictate its design.

However, dependency inversion should not be interpreted as requiring an interface for every class. An abstraction is useful when it represents a meaningful boundary, enables substitution, or isolates an important source of change.

## 1.4 Clean Architecture versus SOLID

Clean Architecture draws heavily on SOLID principles, especially the Dependency Inversion Principle.

SOLID primarily provides guidance for object and module design.

Clean Architecture applies related principles to system-level boundaries.

For example\:

- Single Responsibility helps separate business use cases.
- Interface Segregation encourages focused contracts.
- Dependency Inversion prevents domain logic from depending directly on infrastructure.

A system can use SOLID principles without adopting the full Clean Architecture model.

Likewise, having four projects named `Domain`, `Application`, `Infrastructure`, and `API` does not guarantee that a system follows Clean Architecture.

### Leadership perspective

At the Principal Engineer level, the goal is not to enforce a textbook diagram.

It is to answer\:

**Which parts of our system must remain stable as technologies, teams, and business requirements evolve?**

Those are the boundaries worth protecting.

# Module 2 — Layers and dependency management

30 minutes

## 2.1 The four common layers

Clean Architecture is frequently implemented using four conceptual layers, although exact project boundaries vary.

**Presentation / API**

HTTP endpoints, request mapping, authentication entry points

**Application**

Use cases, orchestration, ports, transaction coordination

**Domain**

Entities, value objects, invariants, business policies

---

**Infrastructure**

Database, messaging, storage, external service adapters

Implements contracts owned by inner layers

Infrastructure is shown separately because it depends inward on application/domain contracts; it is not necessarily a layer that the application references directly.

## 2.2 Domain layer

The domain represents the business model and its rules.

Typical components include\:

- Entities with identity and lifecycle.
- Value objects representing meaningful concepts.
- Aggregates enforcing consistency boundaries.
- Domain services for rules that do not naturally belong to one entity.
- Domain events representing business occurrences.

Consider an account balance rule.

```csharp
public sealed class Account
{
    public decimal Balance { get; private set; }

    public void Withdraw(decimal amount)
    {
        if (amount <= 0)
            throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(amount));

        if (Balance < amount)
            throw new InsufficientFundsException();

        Balance -= amount;
    }
}
```

The important architectural detail is what this code does **not** know about.

It does not know about\:

- SQL Server.
- Entity Framework.
- HTTP.
- Kafka.
- Azure.
- JSON serialization.

It only knows the business invariant.

In a production financial system, this would also need appropriate currency modeling and concurrency control. The example illustrates domain encapsulation, not a complete transaction design.

### Why domain independence matters

If the organization migrates from SQL Server to PostgreSQL, the business rule should remain unchanged.

If an API becomes a background-processing workflow, the rule should remain unchanged.

If a new frontend is introduced, the rule should remain unchanged.

That is the value of isolating domain policy.

## 2.3 Application layer

The application layer coordinates business use cases.

For example\:

```text
TransferFunds
    ↓
Load accounts
    ↓
Validate transfer policy
    ↓
Apply debit and credit
    ↓
Commit transaction
    ↓
Arrange notification/event publication
```

The application layer decides **what sequence of operations accomplishes the use case**\.

The domain decides **which business operations are valid**\.

This distinction matters.

A domain entity should not normally be responsible for initiating database transactions, calling an email provider, or publishing messages.

Those are application or infrastructure responsibilities.

### Domain versus application rules

| Domain responsibility | Application responsibility |
|--------|--------|
| A transfer amount must be positive | Retrieve the source and destination accounts |
| An account cannot violate its balance policy | Coordinate transaction boundaries |
| An order cannot ship before payment | Invoke a payment gateway |
| A subscription has an expiration policy | Schedule a renewal workflow |
| A tenant must not exceed its contracted entitlement | Obtain tenant context and coordinate entitlement checks |

The distinction is not always perfectly clear. What matters is making responsibilities explicit and maintaining consistency.

## 2.4 Infrastructure layer

Infrastructure handles interactions with external systems.

Examples include\:

- EF Core implementations of persistence contracts.
- Kafka producers and consumers.
- Azure Blob Storage adapters.
- SMTP or third-party email gateways.
- Redis caching implementations.
- External identity and authorization integrations.

Suppose the application needs to notify a customer.

The application defines\:

```csharp
public interface INotificationSender
{
    Task SendAsync(
        Notification notification,
        CancellationToken cancellationToken);
}
```

Infrastructure can implement the contract using an SMTP relay, Azure Communication Services, or another provider.

The use case depends on the business capability of sending a notification, not a specific provider's SDK.

An important nuance: interfaces should express application needs rather than simply mirror every method of an infrastructure library.

## 2.5 Presentation layer

The presentation layer exposes the application to consumers.

It can be\:

- ASP.NET Core controllers or minimal APIs.
- gRPC endpoints.
- Message consumers.
- Background jobs.
- Command-line tools.

A well-designed API endpoint generally handles transport-specific concerns, maps the request into an application operation, and maps the result back to an HTTP response.

It should not become the primary location for business rules.

### The composition root

At application startup, the outermost layer wires implementations to contracts using dependency injection.

```csharp
builder.Services.AddScoped<
    INotificationSender,
    SmtpNotificationSender>();
```

The application references the abstraction.

The runtime receives the implementation.

**This is how dependency inversion and dependency injection work together.** They are related but different concepts: dependency inversion is an architectural principle; dependency injection is one way to supply dependencies.

## 2.6 Dependencies versus execution flow

This is one of the most commonly misunderstood concepts.

**Runtime execution**

API

Use Case

SQL Adapter

---

**Compile-time dependencies**

```svg
<svg viewBox="0 0 320 115" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="117" y="4" width="92" height="37" rx="7" fill="#276EA7" /><text x="163" y="27" text-anchor="middle" fill="white" font-size="12">Application</text><rect x="9" y="74" width="104" height="34" rx="7" fill="#9ABBD7" fill-opacity=".28" stroke="#6A94B7" /><rect x="207" y="74" width="104" height="34" rx="7" fill="#9ABBD7" fill-opacity=".28" stroke="#6A94B7" /><text x="61" y="95" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-size="12">API</text><text x="259" y="95" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-size="12">Infrastructure</text><g stroke="#3879AE" stroke-width="2" fill="none" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><path d="M61 73 L117 38 M109 38 L117 38 L114 47" /><path d="M259 73 L209 38 M212 47 L209 38 L218 40" /></g></svg>
```

Both API and infrastructure depend on application contracts. The application does not need a source-code reference to the infrastructure implementation.

The application may invoke an infrastructure implementation at runtime without referencing its concrete type.

This is foundational to understanding Clean Architecture correctly.

# Module 3 — Enterprise implementation patterns

35 minutes

## 3.1 Applying Clean Architecture to an enterprise platform

Consider an internal feature flag management platform used by hundreds of engineers.

The platform must support\:

- Creating and updating feature flags.
- Enforcing environment-specific rules.
- Managing user permissions.
- Scheduling deployments.
- Producing reports.
- Auditing changes.

A possible design\:

```text
FeatureFlag.Api
    Controllers
    Authentication
    Request/Response Models

FeatureFlag.Application
    CreateFeatureFlag
    UpdateFeatureFlag
    CompareEnvironments
    ScheduleDeployment
    Authorization Policies
    Repository / Gateway Interfaces

FeatureFlag.Domain
    FeatureFlag
    Environment
    DeploymentSchedule
    Business Invariants

FeatureFlag.Infrastructure
    SqlFeatureFlagRepository
    IdentityProviderAdapter
    AuditEventPublisher
    ReportingQueries
```

The objective is not merely placing classes in different assemblies.

It is ensuring that a change to the identity provider or reporting database does not require rewriting the core rules for creating and deploying feature flags.

## 3.2 Commands, queries, and CQRS

Clean Architecture and CQRS are complementary but independent.

CQRS separates operations that change state from operations that retrieve information.

For example\:

**Commands**

- CreateFeatureFlag
- EnableFeatureFlag
- ScheduleDeployment

**Queries**

- GetFeatureFlag
- CompareEnvironments
- GetUpcomingDeployments

This separation can be valuable because commands and queries have different requirements.

Commands often need domain validation, concurrency handling, and transactional consistency.

Queries often need efficient joins, projections, pagination, and reporting.

### A critical architectural trade-off

Some teams force all reporting queries through rich domain aggregates.

That can lead to\:

- Excessive database round trips.
- Unnecessary object hydration.
- Complex repository interfaces.
- Poor reporting performance.

A more pragmatic approach is to allow read-only queries to use optimized projections or SQL directly from an appropriate application-facing query adapter.

Clean Architecture does not require every database read to pass through a rich domain model.

The important boundary is preventing infrastructure-specific concerns from contaminating business policies.

## 3.3 Repositories and the EF Core question

One recurring architectural debate is whether every application should wrap EF Core behind repository interfaces.

There is no universal answer.

EF Core already provides repository-like and unit-of-work capabilities through `DbSet` and `DbContext`\.

Adding another abstraction can be useful when\:

- The application requires persistence independence.
- Aggregate persistence needs a clear contract.
- Tests benefit from substituting a focused persistence port.
- Multiple persistence implementations are genuinely possible.
- Domain logic must be isolated from EF Core.

However, a generic repository like this\:

```csharp
IRepository<T>
```

with universal CRUD methods may add little value and can hide useful EF Core capabilities.

### Practical comparison

| Approach | Advantages | Disadvantages |
|--------|--------|--------|
| Direct DbContext in use cases | Simple, efficient, full EF Core features | Application becomes coupled to EF Core |
| Specific repository interfaces | Explicit boundaries, domain-oriented operations | More interfaces and implementations |
| Generic repository | Consistent basic CRUD abstraction | Often leaky and overly generic |
| Hybrid persistence | Optimized reads, protected write model | Requires disciplined conventions |

For many enterprise applications, a hybrid approach is reasonable.

Use domain-oriented repositories where aggregate boundaries and business rules matter. Use optimized query adapters for reporting and data-heavy read operations.

## 3.4 Clean Architecture in microservices

Clean Architecture and microservices solve different problems.

- **Clean Architecture** governs dependencies and responsibilities inside a software system.
- **Microservices architecture** governs the decomposition, deployment, and communication of independently operated services.

A microservice can use Clean Architecture internally.

A modular monolith can also use Clean Architecture.

In fact, a well-structured modular monolith often provides stronger starting boundaries than prematurely splitting a system into many services.

### Example: customer notification platform

Imagine a notification service with\:

- Kafka consumers.
- Email delivery rules.
- SMTP relay integration.
- Redis-based rate limiting.
- SQL persistence.
- Retry and failure handling.

A Clean Architecture design might separate\:

| Concern | Primary ownership |
|--------|--------|
| Notification eligibility rules | Domain |
| Delivery workflow | Application |
| Kafka consumption and publishing | Infrastructure / entry adapter |
| SMTP provider integration | Infrastructure |
| Redis rate limiter implementation | Infrastructure |
| Delivery policy and rate-limit decisions | Domain or application |
| Health endpoints | Presentation / infrastructure |
| Dependency injection | Composition root |

The key is to distinguish a business policy from its technical implementation.

For example, the policy that a customer may receive no more than a contracted number of messages is a business rule.

The Redis algorithm used to enforce that policy across instances is an infrastructure mechanism.
